3.text: swallowed the body a fourth time, warmed it in his stomach, and spat it out again on the skin.

4.text: Then he flung the soul at it. “Oh, oh, oh!” sighed the boy, and then sat up on the skin.

5.text: Instances of the swallowing of souls and bodies of men by shamans

6.text: frequently occur in Chukchee tales. Thus Kukuˊlpɪn, in one of the tales,

7.text: when visiting the interior of America, swallows his companion and a young

8.text: girl, and, turning into a bird, carries them to his home.¹ In the tale of the

9.text: Contest of Two Shamans, a small bird, Perruˊper (Uria Brünnichi), acting as

10.text: an assistant keˊlᴇ of one of the shamans, comes to the house of the other

11.text: one, which is watched by a host of his keˊlet. The bird dives under

12.text: ground and succeeds in pushing the point of its beak through the middle of

13.text: the floor, then with one drawn-in breath, one whoop, it pulls him down and

14.text: swallows him under the very eyes of his house-mates.²

15.text: During the process of bringing back the lost soul of the patient, the

16.text: soul is spoken of as a “little fellow” (tuˊmg̣ᴀqäi), and the shaman is called

18.text: Sometimes, however, the shaman refuses to put the soul back personally,

19.text: and, instead of that, orders the mother or the sister of the patient, or, in

20.text: their absence, the father or the brother, more rarely the wife, to go out at

21.text: dawn the next morning, and to pick up a blade of grass somewhere near

22.text: by, repeating, “Here, here, here, I found the ‘little fellow,’ be you under

23.text: my power!” This grass represents the “little fellow,” and it must be tied

24.text: to the collar-strings of the patient.

25.text: Another method of shamanistic treatment of diseases may be called

26.text: “magic surgery.” In this the shaman pretends to operate on the diseased

27.text: part of the body and to set it right, removing the pus and the bad blood,

28.text: and sometimes even recasting the whole limb. The shaman acts in a way

29.text: somewhat similar to that described in regard to the recovering of a lost soul;

30.text: that is, he puts his face close down to the body of the patient, blows on it,

31.text: or sucks for some time a fold of the skin. It is supposed that the keˊlᴇ

32.text: who assists him is able to extract and to eat up the source of the illness.

33.text: Some of the rubbing and sucking has the character of massage, especially in

34.text: the treatment of swellings and bruises. The shaman often produces a beetle,

35.text: a thorn, or even a small stone, which he pretends to have extracted from

36.text: the body. The same cure may be carried out also by means of various

37.text: incantations, which will be described in the next chapter.

38.text: Besides this, the shaman pretends to possess the power to open the

39.text: abdomen of the patient in order to inspect the internal organs, to remove

40.text: the stricken parts, and then to make the wound whole again. This can be

41.text: done only with a special knife strengthened by various incantations. Moreover,
